reviews.title: NGUYỄN TRẦN KHÁNH LY · IELTS 49 · W07 · Đề 1
reviews.overall: Em viết đúng đề, đủ 182 từ và chia hai đoạn Detail theo mốc 2006 hợp lý. Các số liệu em nêu đều khớp bảng, nhưng hai nhận định về mức cao nhất và thấp nhất của toàn bảng lại sai: Thailand đạt đỉnh vào 2006, còn mức thấp nhất là Argentina vào 2003. Overview cũng chưa cho thấy Thailand tăng rồi giảm. Cô yêu cầu em sửa các so sánh này, đổi từ nối ở câu về Argentina năm 2009 và đọc lại từng câu để số liệu, xu hướng và lời kết luận thống nhất.
reviews.dataGrouping: Em chia Detail 1 cho giai đoạn 2003–2006 và Detail 2 cho giai đoạn 2006–2009; mỗi đoạn có ít nhất hai câu và đều nhắc đến ba nước. Cách chia này giúp thấy Argentina vượt Australia vào 2006 và Thailand đảo chiều sau mốc đó. Em cần giữ rõ giới hạn so sánh theo từng năm, vì số của năm 2009 không tự là cực trị của cả bảng.

reviews.originalEssay:
The given table illustrates how many cars were manufactured in Argentina, Australia and Thailand over a period of six years, commencing from 2003.
Overall, there was a general increase in the number of cars made in Argentina and Thailand, while an opposite trend was observed in the case of Australia. Also of note is that Thailand consistently had the highest figures throughout the years.
To elaborate, in 2003, around 735,852 cars were produced in Thailand, with a subsequent substantial rise to 1,162,356 in 2006. The figures for Australia and Argentina, conversely, moved in different directions, with Australia falling from 452,163 to 341,268, while Argentina experienced a growth from 235,088 to 352,759 during the same period of time.
Regarding the latter half of the provided timeline, the number of cars produced in Thailand went down to 999,963 in 2009, which still marked the highest point of the entire table. A growth was, likewise, recorded in the figures for Argentina, reaching 466,089 in 2009. Finally, the production of Australia kept declining to 245,624 in 2009, which was obviously the lowest over the whole table.

Overall, there was a general increase in the number of male prisoners, while an opposite trend was observed in the case of female prisoners. Also of note is that male prisoners consistently had the highest figures throughout the years.
To elaborate, in 1911, around 20,000 male prisoners were recorded, with a subsequent drop to 10,000 in 1931 before going back to 20,000 in 1951 and 1961. The figures for female prisoners, conversely, fell from over 3,000 in 1911 to a low of under 1,000 in 1941 during the same period of time.
Regarding the latter half of the provided timeline, the number of male prisoners continued to go up, and to a far greater extent, reaching over 40,000 in 2001, which marked the highest point of the entire chart. A growth was, likewise, recorded in the figures for female prisoners, rising to around 2,000 in 2001. Finally, the population of female prisoners remained lower than that of males over the whole graph.

reviews.suggestedRevision:
The two line charts compare the numbers of male and female prisoners in a European country from 1911 to 2001.

Overall, the male prison population was higher throughout the period. After an early decline, it recovered and then rose sharply, especially between 1971 and 1981. By contrast, the female population fell steeply until 1941, fluctuated afterwards and ended below its initial level.

For men, the figure was approximately 18,000 in both 1911 and 1921 before dropping to about 10,000 in 1931. It returned to around 19,000 in 1951 and remained close to 20,000 until 1971. The number then jumped to roughly 39,000 in 1981 and climbed further to about 46,000 by 2001.

For women, the number fell from around 3,200 in 1911 to its lowest point of about 500 in 1941. It subsequently rose to approximately 1,500 in 1961, followed by another fall to around 700 in 1971. Despite a later recovery to roughly 1,900 in 2001, it remained well below the corresponding male figure.

The given line chart illustrates the proportion of female members of parliament in five European countries over a 12-year period, commencing from 2000.
Overall, out of the studied nations, only France witnessed signs of fluctuation in its percentage of female parliament members, while the figures for the remaining countries experienced an upward trend. Despite this, Italy finished with the highest figure by the end of the period.  
To elaborate, in 2000, an impressive 34% of the total parliamentary seats in Germany was reported as held by women, followed by Italy at 26% and France at 25%. The figure for Italy went up by roughly 14% over the whole timeline, thereby allowing this nation to maintain its dominance with 40% in 2012, while Germany grew steadily to 38%. The figure for France, however, fell slightly before recovering gradually, undergoing a fluctuation between 25% and 37%.  
Regarding the remaining, the most noticeable upturn was seen in the UK, rising from around 4% in 2000 to an impressive nearly 30% after 12 years, making it second only to Germany, Italy, and France in terms of female representation for most of the period. The figures for Belgium also grew from 17% to more or less 29% for the same period of time, yet they remained among the lowest over the chart.

The given pie charts illustrate the primary reasons why students chose a particular university in the UK over a 10-year period, commencing from 1997.
Overall, suitable degree courses had the highest figures throughout the period. Additionally, out of the studied reasons, good sports and social activities witnessed the most significant decline.

Regarding the remaining reasons, quality of resources fell from 21% in 1997 to 17% in 2007. Good sports and social activities also witnessed signs of a sharp decline, dropping from 19% to just 6% over the same period, making it the least popular reason in the final year.

The given table illustrates the percentages of the population aged 65 and above in three different countries from 1988 to 2000 and predictions until 2030.  
Overall, it is expected that there will be an increase in the proportion of elderly people in all three nations over the period shown. Equally notably, Germany records the highest figures throughout the surveyed years.  
To elaborate, in 1988, Germany had the largest share of population aged 65 and over, at 20.35%, followed by a steady rise to 25.53% in 2000 and a final anticipation of a further increase to 30.65% in 2030.
